title: Eight Chapters
hook: his introduction to Pirkei Avot, on the soul's health

segments.voice: Yesterday, the critics of the list, and your line: not everyone agreed. Did you try naming what you take from someone before naming where you differ? Today, back to Maimonides, and another doorway in his commentary. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

Sweet tastes bitter. Bitter tastes sweet. A person with a sick body, Maimonides writes, can lose their sense of taste so badly that they crave what harms them and turn away from what would heal them. He knew bodies. He worked as a physician. But in this passage he isn't writing about the body. He's writing about the soul. And he says the same thing happens there. Today, the little book where he says it, written as a doorway into Pirkei Avot.
screen: `SWEET TASTES BITTER.` → `A PHYSICIAN'S PICTURE.` → `NOW, THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Shemonah Perakim. Eight Chapters. Maimonides wrote them as an introduction to Pirkei Avot, the Mishnah's tractate of sayings about how to live. Before he explains the sayings, he wants you to understand the one who will practice them: the human soul. Take it in steps. First, the soul has health and sickness, just like a body. A healthy soul tends toward good actions and finds them natural. A sick soul tends toward harmful ones, and, like the sick tongue, may even call them sweet. Second, a sick person needs a doctor, and doesn't trust their own cravings. So too, he says, a person whose soul is unwell should go to the wise, who are physicians of souls, and let them help. Third, the cure is practice. Traits are changed the way health is restored: by doing, again and again, until a new habit takes hold. Pirkei Avot, read this way, is a book of medicine. Fourth, where he gathered it. In his introduction he says plainly that these ideas aren't all his own. He drew on the sages and on the philosophers, and he tells the reader to hear the truth from whoever says it. A physician uses the remedy that works, whoever found it. That's the doorway into Avot: not a rulebook, a clinic. The soul's health.
screen: `THE SOUL CAN BE WELL OR UNWELL.` · `THE WISE ARE PHYSICIANS OF SOULS.` · `THE CURE IS PRACTICE.` · `HEAR THE TRUTH FROM WHOEVER SAYS IT.` · then, large: `THE SOUL'S HEALTH.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice one trait in yourself, the way a kind doctor notices a symptom. Settle, and let your breath slow. Think back over the last few days. Is there a habit of the heart that keeps showing up? Impatience, worry, a quick tongue, holding back. Don't scold yourself. Just name it, plainly, the way you'd say a knee is sore. Then ask: when does it flare up? Hold that question for a few breaths. Then let it go, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Shemonah Perakim. Eight Chapters. Maimonides' introduction to Pirkei Avot, treating the soul as something that can be well or unwell, and healed by practice. Today's word.
Your line: the soul's health. Today, when the trait you named shows up, don't fight it. Just note the time and the place, like a doctor keeping a chart. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Shemonah Perakim is studied as an introduction to Pirkei Avot, a text some communities read chapter by chapter on Shabbat afternoons between Passover and Shavuot, and some through the summer.
